## Historical context

By 2020, several long-running shifts converged. The Iranian regional posture — proxy networks across Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen — had hardened into what Hammad calls the axis of resistance and was the principal security concern of Gulf monarchies. The 2015 JCPOA's collapse, US withdrawal in 2018, and increasing US-Iranian tensions had aligned Gulf-Israeli threat perceptions more closely than at any prior point. Saudi-led changes since 2015 had relaxed the prior taboo on contact with Israel within Sunni Gulf elite networks. The Trump administration made Israeli normalization a central regional initiative, offering significant inducements — F-35 sales to the UAE, removing Sudan from the US state-sponsors-of-terrorism list, US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. The signing ceremony took place at the White House on September 15, 2020, with the United Arab Emirates and the Kingdom of Bahrain joining Israel in a joint declaration; bilateral treaties between UAE-Israel and Bahrain-Israel were signed the same day. Sudan and Morocco joined later in 2020. Saudi Arabia did not sign, though press reporting and subsequent diplomacy suggested that a Saudi-Israeli framework was under active negotiation until October 7, 2023.

## What the document says (in plain English)

The Abraham Accords Declaration itself is a short, ceremonial document signed by the four parties — the United States, Israel, the UAE, and Bahrain. It commits the parties to the pursuit of peace, mutual understanding, and coexistence; affirms the importance of maintaining and strengthening peace based on mutual recognition and respect; and commits the parties to peaceful and diplomatic resolution of disputes. It does not specify substantive provisions. The substance is in the two **bilateral treaties** signed alongside it: the Treaty of Peace, Diplomatic Relations and Full Normalization between the UAE and Israel, and the Declaration of Peace, Cooperation, and Constructive Diplomatic and Friendly Relations between Bahrain and Israel. These bilateral instruments establish full diplomatic relations, embassies, direct flights, trade and investment frameworks, cooperation in security, energy, technology, and tourism, and visa-free travel for citizens. Crucially, the bilateral instruments do not condition normalization on Israeli concessions to the Palestinians. The UAE statement referenced an Israeli commitment to suspend (not cancel) planned annexation of parts of the West Bank — a commitment whose substantive content was disputed within hours of the signing.

## Key terms and ambiguities

The decisive feature is what the Accords **do not** say. They contain no reference to UNSC 242's land-for-peace formula as a precondition; no reference to a Palestinian state; no reference to the API's integrated linkage. The Palestinian Authority denounced the Accords as a betrayal of the API consensus; the UAE responded that suspension of West Bank annexation was a Palestinian gain. The contested term is **"suspension"** of annexation: was this a binding Israeli commitment, a unilateral political statement, or merely a temporary postponement of measures Israel was unlikely to take regardless? The diplomatic record supports something closer to the third reading. A second contested feature is whether the Accords represent a **decoupling** of the two diplomatic tracks (the Israeli reading, the UAE reading) or a **unilateral abandonment** of the Palestinian track by Arab states (the Palestinian and Iranian reading). Hammad's lectures emphasize that both readings can be true simultaneously, and that this dual character is what makes the Accords structurally significant.

## Hammad-frame connections

The Abraham Accords are the central evidence for Hammad's [Gause frame](../frames/gause.qmd) argument about regional realignment from pan-Arab collective politics to bilateral state-led security politics. They are also a [Bellin frame](../frames/bellin.qmd) case in the survival logic of Gulf monarchies under perceived Iranian pressure. The Accords are the empirical anchor for the post-2020 portion of the [Abraham Accords deep dive](../abraham-accords.qmd) and for the recognition-track half of the [Nash equilibrium](../nash-equilibrium.qmd) analysis.

## How to deploy this in an essay

If your prompt mentions **normalization**, **alliance reordering**, **the Saudi track**, **the post-Iran-deal regional system**, or **Q3, Q7, Q8, Q9**, cite the Abraham Accords with date September 15, 2020, and the one-line significance: UAE-Bahrain-Israel full diplomatic normalization without prior Palestinian settlement, breaking the Arab Peace Initiative's linkage rule. The mistake students make is to overstate the Accords' immediate substantive effect (the bilateral economic flows are real but modest) and to understate their structural effect (the API's collective-bargaining logic is now optional, not mandatory). Pair with the API for the pivot story. Citable phrasing: full UAE-Bahrain-Israel normalization, with annexation suspended but not cancelled, and no precondition on Palestinian statehood.
